fatal_errors: It selects conventional tempered martensitic steel rather than the target AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
It incorrectly excludes compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys, although the central result is a ductile–brittle–ductile transition in precisely such an alloy.

It attributes embrittlement to grain-boundary impurity segregation instead of enhanced L12 ordering, elevated antiphase-boundary energy, planar slip, and stress concentration at jagged B2/FCC phase boundaries.
It does not reconstruct the approximately 600°C embrittlement condition or the approximately 750°C ductility-recovery condition.
It partly conflates aging temperature with mechanical-test temperature and gives an unsupported high-temperature recovery explanation based on enhanced dislocation activity.
explanation: The hypothesis captures only the generic non-monotonic ductile–brittle–ductile outcome and proposes a testable experiment for classical temper embrittlement. It otherwise describes the conventional-alloy baseline that the target work contrasts against. The required material is as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with FCC and B2 phases, aged within roughly 550–750°C. Maximum embrittlement near 600°C arises from strong L12 ordering in FCC domains and jagged B2/FCC boundaries, whereas reduced ordering and ductile transition zones restore ductility near 750°C. No cited evidence supports the proposed alternative, and its categorical claim that the phenomenon is inapplicable to HEAs directly contradicts the target.
